claim: Pennington and Hastie's founding evidence is about one person building an account from one case (interview N=26, 16 analysed; order study N=130; N=414), with no deliberation measured, and the authors say the interview may have invited story-telling.
agent_test: Scope note only: score single-agent account building, not group claims.

claim: Presenting the same evidence in story order versus witness order moves individual verdicts by large amounts (guilty 31% to 78% across cells; row means 69 vs 47; column means 45 vs 70; N=130); a replication with different materials exists (Smith 1988, cited, not opened).
agent_test: Give the agent the same case file in chronological-causal and by-source order at equal tokens; measure answer flip rate and confidence.

claim: Order effects on legal judgment also appear in later work (case order, five studies, n=1,023) but are asymmetric and sometimes reverse direction, so order sensitivity must be measured per task.
agent_test: Run each item under 2+ random evidence orders; report order sensitivity and treat flips as low confidence.

claim: Nearly half of story content is inferred, not given (45% of protocol references), and mock jurors falsely recognise verdict-consistent inferred sentences.
agent_test: Count inferred items in the agent's account; check each against source text; compare accuracy with and without that check.

claim: Jurors cover the legal checklist only partly while relying on a narrative summary (75% of 20 students; few cover all elements), supporting the formalism critique from inside the theory.
agent_test: Code checks every required element of the task; compare with story-only judgment.

claim: Answer menu changes verdicts: three-verdict systems cut conviction odds (OR 0.625, CI 0.51-0.77; 28.7% vs 39.2%; 10 trials, 1778 jurors).
agent_test: Vary number and wording of answer options at equal tokens; fix the menu in all arms. (a21 and b08 are the same paper.)

claim: Verdict procedure matters even after deliberation: special-verdict (question-by-question) forms shift outcomes versus general verdicts, in lone readers and groups.
agent_test: Compare holistic and element-wise answering of the same case by the agent; log disagreement.

claim: Real juries show decision-threshold effects: in Louisiana fewer than 1% ended 9-to-convict vs 17% exactly 10 (n=1,960, chi2=91.18); experiments show being pivotal raises punitive votes, but not acquittal votes.
agent_test: Record whether a stop rule ended the search; compare belief before and after the stop rule is applied.

claim: Human deliberation can wash out a minority: in a pilot, 6 of 6 initial not-guilty voters ended guilty (7 juries, 34 paired, McNemar p=0.031); mechanism not separable.
agent_test: Not directly testable; use as caution against counting convergence as evidence. (a14 and b13 are the same paper.)

claim: Misinformation from fellow jurors is often remembered as trial evidence and a judicial warning did nothing (only 6.5% could report it); in a reanalysis memory entry exceeded judgment impact.
agent_test: Tag each claim's source; test whether a source tag beats a warning prompt at equal tokens.

claim: In LLM mock juries seeded 11-1, almost no one moves: 17 of 18 runs hung. Full text shows temperature fixed at 0.9, two models, N=3 per cell, and persona retained even in the no-vote arm, so the cause (RLHF, persona, or stop rule) cannot be assigned.
agent_test: Run independent attempts without chat and compare with a debate arm at equal tokens.

claim: Multi-agent debate of homogeneous LLMs does not beat self-correction or majority vote and costs more tokens (Ministral GSM-Hard debate 20.7% vs self-correction 48.3%; majority-vote accuracy 77.35% in both arms; 57% more tokens; 2.1-3.4x tokens).
agent_test: Equal-token comparison: N independent attempts plus code check versus N-agent debate.

claim: Peer pressure on LLMs depends on count and framing, and one structured dissenter cuts yield by 54-73 points (user-role 4v0 80.25%; 3v1 12.75%).
agent_test: Add a protected dissent slot; compare yield on planted wrong peer answers with and without it.

claim: Prompt instructions to be open-minded or to resist consensus are unreliable levers: effect depends on model (Llama 2.0 to 6.0 vote changes; GPT-4o flat), and claims like 'three reviewers disagree' flip judges 25-71%.
agent_test: Compare a prose doubt instruction with a code-triggered check at equal tokens.

claim: A changed answer is not proof of persuasion: 37% of pairs change under self-reflection alone and only part of peer adoption is correction.
agent_test: Count a revision as valid only if tied to a failing check or new evidence; audit the rate.

claim: LLM juror simulations at scale test only the single-juror step; emotional statements often make verdicts harsher and background match drives changes (432K decisions, 20 LLMs; 12 human raters on 25 cases).
agent_test: Strip persona and background from the scoring step; verify verdict invariance.

claim: No study found tests story-model predictions (story form, story building) on LLMs. Nearest work: two LLM studies show recency order effects on legal judgments (GPT-4o/GPT-5.2 guilt ratings; six LLMs on 657 civil cases) but they vary which side's evidence is last, not story versus source order. Story-versus-source order on LLMs remains untested.
agent_test: Run an order-manipulation test on our own logs.

claim: A formal reconstruction (Urbaniak 2017) adds coverage, missing evidence, exclusion between rival stories and exhaustion as checkable criteria, partly answering why story form might matter.
agent_test: Implement per-evidence-item plausibility under each story as coded coverage; compare to holistic scoring.

claim: A coded story-coverage audit (cite every claim, audit gaps) improves factual consistency in an agent (coverage 0.9014 vs 0.8436 without audit; +20.35% consistency), in synthetic scenarios. A related non-legal result: list-then-verify closed checks raise omission detection (clinical notes, paired discrimination 0.79-0.94 on added content vs 0.50-0.63 on omissions for monolithic judges), but this is judge discrimination, not answer accuracy at equal tokens.
agent_test: Add a citation-coverage check to the agent; measure accuracy at equal tokens.

claim: Closing hypotheses early is the main failure in causal reconstruction; the best-fitting story crowds out rivals, and a weak counter-story can raise confidence in the favourite.
agent_test: Require two live hypotheses until a named test discriminates; compare error rates.

claim: The story form itself has no demonstrated causal role beyond structure; no experiment compares story format with an equally coherent non-story format, and the model's group-deliberation claims are unsupported.
agent_test: Compare a structured causal chain with a prose narrative of the same content.

claim: The first-ballot-majority figure is verified as a secondary report: majority on the first ballot matched the verdict in 90% of cases in a 225-juror retrospective sample (Kalven & Zeisel 1966, via Diamond et al. 2010). It is a weak figure: jurors often do not take an immediate vote (3% to 31% of real juries, 21% and 28% in two simulations), and Kalven and Zeisel called it a 'radical hunch'. Lab hung rates are 21% vs under 10% in real juries.
agent_test: Record the true first answer before any critique step, then report how often the final answer equals it, at equal tokens against a no-critique arm.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-10 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Coherence-based shifts: evidence is rated higher after the favoured answer is formed (human, N=83 preprint). In LLMs the nearest evidence is choice-supportive bias: confidence in an answer rises when the model sees its own earlier choice, and change-of-mind rate falls from 32.5% to 13.1% (Kumaran et al. 2025, binary geography questions). Evidence-rating shifts in LLMs are not directly tested.
agent_test: Rate evidence before showing the candidate answer; compare ratings after exposure.

claim: LLMs show recency in evidence order on legal tasks: guilt ratings were higher when incriminating evidence came last (GPT-4o order F(1,711)=424.76, GPT-5.2 F(1,711)=71.24, N=720 trials each), and six LLMs favoured the party whose evidence came last in 657 civil cases. Legal-expert and careful-reasoning prompts did not remove it, and justify-from-the-case raised it (beta=0.39).
agent_test: Run each item under 2+ evidence orders; count order flips; prefer structure over instructions.

claim: Debate cost and benefit values are confirmed from full text: Ministral GSM-Hard debate 20.7% vs self-correction 48.3% at 23,816 vs 10,707 tokens; majority-vote accuracy 77.35% for both self-reflection and full-reasoning debate (+57% tokens); one dissenter at 3v1 holds yield at 12.75% against 80.25% at 4v0.
agent_test: Score majority accuracy at equal tokens; use self-reflection as the baseline.

claim: Protected dissent versus code-triggered recheck at equal tokens has not been tested. Matched-ceiling work shows no protocol wins everywhere (each of four cells had a different winner) and vote-entropy escalation gains +1.6 pp (p=0.125).
agent_test: Run both arms at equal tokens on 100+ items.

claim: The McKenzie, Lee and Chen (2002) effect (weak case for one side raises confidence in the opposing side) is known only from its abstract here; exact numbers and any LLM test are missing.
agent_test: Score a self-generated rival's strength before showing it; check whether it raises the favoured answer.

claim: Replications of the story-order effect (Smith 1988 and others) and a matched non-story structure test were not found; the story-order effect stays single-study and the claim that story form itself matters stays unproven.
agent_test: Test story order, source order and a matched causal list at equal tokens.
